video_title: Saronic's 4 Co-Founders on Building a $9.25B Shipbuilder | Part III
gist: An on-site tour of autonomous shipbuilder Saronic ($9.25B valuation, $2.6B raised, ~4 years old) in which co-founders lay out the hard numbers of the US-China shipbuilding gap (230:1 overall, 1,000+ commercial ships vs 5 in 2024, China at 57% of global capacity) and the operational playbook they are using to close it: unmanned-first hardware/software co-design, modular shipyard construction at the $3B Port Alpha, and pre-buying scarce US aluminum and steel. Only three co-founders (COO Doug, CCO Rob, CTO Viv) are interviewed in this part despite the title's '4 Co-Founders'; the opening stats segment is delivered by an unnamed co-founder.

insights.claim: China outbuilds the United States in shipbuilding by roughly 230 to 1 in aggregate, but the gap is only about 6-to-1 or 7-to-1 in warships (US launches 5-10 military vessels a year versus China's ~30) — the true discrepancy is commercial.
insights.speaker: Saronic co-founder, opening segment
insights.so_what: The headline 230:1 statistic used to justify defense-shipbuilding budgets is driven by commercial tonnage, so policy that targets only naval yards will not close the industrial-capacity gap.
insights.quote: China outbuilds the US 230 to 1

insights.claim: China built over a thousand large ocean-going commercial vessels in 2024 while the United States built five.
insights.speaker: Saronic co-founder, opening segment
insights.so_what: Quantifies the collapse of US commercial yard capacity — the base load that keeps naval yards, welders and suppliers viable.
insights.quote: They build over a thousand commercial ships last year. And the United States built five.

insights.claim: China holds 57% of total global shipbuilding capacity and is taking capacity from the rest of the world by undercutting on price in the commercial market, with its entire shipbuilding industry subsidized across construction, raw materials, labor and free shipyard financing.
insights.speaker: Saronic co-founder, opening segment
insights.so_what: A subsidized-price mechanism, not efficiency, is driving the capacity shift — meaning tariffs or allied reshoring subsidies are the plausible policy response and a tailwind for domestic yards.
insights.quote: Their entire shipbuilding industry is completely subsidized. Not only direct construction subsidies, but they subsidize the raw materials, they subsidize the labor, and they basically give them free financing for these shipyards.

insights.claim: Allied shipbuilding is not a fallback: South Korea and Japan, the world's next two largest shipbuilders, are themselves sourcing a lot of their commercial modules and labor from China, so allied capacity erodes alongside US capacity.
insights.speaker: Saronic co-founder, opening segment
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'build in allied yards' thesis that underpins several Korean and Japanese shipbuilding trades — their supply chains are China-dependent in a conflict scenario.
insights.quote: They're actually on the commercial side, they're actually getting a lot of their modules from China. They're getting a lot of their labor from China.

insights.claim: Naval power has historically been determined by who can build the most ships, not who can build the most exquisite or expensive ones — the explicit founding thesis behind Saronic's cheap, mass-produced autonomous vessels.
insights.speaker: Saronic co-founder, opening segment
insights.so_what: The mental model that separates attritable-mass defense companies from exquisite-platform primes — a structural bet on volume manufacturers over legacy shipbuilders.
insights.quote: what has typically just determined naval power is who can build the the most ships. It's not who can build the most exquisite, the most expensive

insights.claim: Chinese shipbuilding is an opaque market where it is very hard to get reliable information, which limits the ability to verify the capacity comparisons being used to set US policy.
insights.speaker: Saronic co-founder, opening segment
insights.so_what: Data quality caveat for anyone sizing the shipbuilding TAM off Chinese-sourced capacity figures.

insights.claim: Only about 1% of the Department of War's roughly $1 trillion FY26 budget went toward autonomy, despite top-down pressure from the administration and Capitol Hill to buy scalable and economical systems.
insights.speaker: Saronic co-founder, opening segment
insights.so_what: The single most important sizing number for autonomous-defense investors: the addressable budget line is tiny today, so the thesis is entirely about mix shift, not current spend.
insights.quote: for '26. 1% 1% went towards autonomy. So, that that just gives you a sense of how far we actually have to go.

insights.claim: The US naval fleet is shrinking to around 290 ships against a 2018 statutory minimum of 355, which the Navy revised upward to 381 in 2024 — and those counts exclude the unmanned ships the fleet will also need.
insights.speaker: Saronic co-founder, opening segment
insights.so_what: A codified, widening gap between statutory requirement and actual fleet is the structural demand signal for any shipbuilding or USV supplier.

insights.claim: The Navy's 30-year plan to grow from 290 to 381 ships is budgeted at $1.2 trillion, against a presidential budget request of $1.5 trillion — and that assumes the country can execute the plan at all.
insights.speaker: Saronic co-founder, opening segment
insights.so_what: Sizes the cost-reduction prize that autonomous shipbuilders are pitching against; the execution risk in the plan is itself the sales argument.

insights.claim: Aircraft carrier cost estimates are escalating in real time — a figure of $13 billion quoted internally was contradicted by the president quoting $19 billion at an event a week earlier — while each carrier takes over 10 years to build and the schedule keeps slipping.
insights.speaker: Saronic co-founder, opening segment
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of exquisite-platform cost escalation, the wedge that low-cost autonomous vessels use to win budget share.
insights.quote: I I was actually quoting 13 billion dollars for an aircraft carrier, and I was at an event where the president spoke just last week. And he quoted 19 billion dollars.

insights.claim: The addressable customer set for autonomous surface vessels spans all services rather than just the Navy — the Army actually has more boats than the Navy does, and Saronic is also targeting the Marine Corps, Coast Guard, Air Force combat search and rescue, commercial buyers and allied militaries.
insights.speaker: Saronic co-founder, opening segment
insights.so_what: Broadens the revenue base beyond the Navy shipbuilding line item, which is the usual bear case on maritime-only defense startups.
insights.quote: The Army actually has more boats than the Navy does.

insights.claim: Saronic has reached a $9.25 billion valuation on $2.6 billion raised in roughly four years, with around 1,600 people rolling up through the COO's operations organization and a $3 billion Port Alpha shipyard announced.
insights.speaker: Doug, COO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Benchmarks the capital intensity and headcount of a credible defense-manufacturing scale-up for anyone underwriting the sector.

insights.claim: Saronic's product strategy is a deliberate size ladder — two lesser-known predecessors (Spyglass and Cutlass) preceded Corsair, and Marauder is the analogous stepping stone toward 400-foot, 800-foot and even Panamax-class 1,200-foot ships.
insights.speaker: Doug, COO of Saronic
insights.so_what: A concrete roadmap signal: the company intends to move up-tonnage into full ship classes, expanding TAM well beyond small USVs.

insights.claim: Saronic's first autonomous boat was a plastic box bought from Amazon with electronics put in it, which became a 6-foot autonomous boat and then Corsair — evidence that the capital-intensive shipbuilding thesis was validated at near-zero cost first.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: A pattern to look for in hard-tech diligence: cheap proof of the autonomy stack before committing to heavy capex.
insights.quote: our first autonomous boat was like a was like a plastic box we bought from Amazon and put some electronics in it

insights.claim: Saronic closed its first government contract within 90 days of founding via a CRADA — a no-cost cooperative research and development agreement that buys early access to non-public customer requirements in exchange for codifying the relationship and managing IP guidelines.
insights.speaker: Rob, Chief Commercial Officer of Saronic
insights.so_what: A replicable go-to-market unlock for defense startups: a free contracting vehicle that provides requirements visibility before any program of record exists.

insights.claim: Saronic sources requirements bottom-up from fleet-level operators rather than from program executive offices or Capitol Hill, treating the gap between what operators are ordered to do and what they actually have as the gold-standard product signal.
insights.speaker: Rob, Chief Commercial Officer of Saronic
insights.so_what: An operating model that explains why some defense startups beat primes on relevance — worth testing against any defense-tech investment.
insights.quote: It was really finding operators and understanding what are the things you're being asked to do that you have to say yes sir, yes ma'am. And then you look at each other and say, we don't have what we need to be able to do that.

insights.claim: Saronic deliberately fuses program management with growth and business development into one flywheel rather than separating them, because the autonomous maritime community is small enough that program teams and sales teams talk to the exact same customers.
insights.speaker: Rob, Chief Commercial Officer of Saronic
insights.so_what: Org-design detail that compresses the customer feedback loop — a differentiator in a niche market with few buyers.

insights.claim: Saronic had to buy out the vast majority of the aluminum in the Louisiana area simply to build one Marauder, and is now pre-securing the steel pipeline for Port Alpha ahead of need.
insights.speaker: Doug, COO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Regional raw-material markets are thin enough that a single program clears them — bullish for domestic metals suppliers and a real bottleneck on any shipbuilding scale-up.
insights.quote: we wound up buying out a vast majority of the aluminum in the Louisiana area where we went ahead and built a Marauder

insights.claim: Casting and forging are the industries most likely to bottleneck US reindustrialization over the next three to five years because they have largely migrated offshore, while wire harnessing previously done in Ukraine or Mexico is only now starting to come back.
insights.speaker: Doug, COO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Names the specific upstream segments where reshoring capital and pricing power will concentrate — a targeted supply-chain trade.
insights.quote: Casting and forging is a big one. You know, I see that being a challenge here in the next 3 to 5 years.

insights.claim: Two decades of certification and qualification requirements in defense manufacturing built a real quality system but also locked a large portion of the American labor force out of the industry — a systemic barrier that must be solved through automated inspection, better work instructions and design simplification rather than more training alone.
insights.speaker: Doug, COO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Reframes the defense labor shortage as a credentialing problem, which is far more tractable — and favors companies investing in inspection automation and part-count reduction.
insights.quote: There's no reason somebody who can't change a tire shouldn't be able to go and build a Corsair or work on a Marauder or work on a larger ship.

insights.claim: The shipyard productivity strategy is to move final outfitting work that traditionally happens on the ship into sub-assemblies built elsewhere, then assemble modules into larger modules into super modules — with robotic aluminum welding from Path Robotics as the enabling partner.
insights.speaker: Doug, COO of Saronic
insights.so_what: The specific manufacturing change that could actually compress shipbuilding cycle times — the operational proof point to watch at Port Alpha.

insights.claim: The hard part of robotic aluminum welding is not tacking metal together but doing it in a way that passes ABS, IMO and Coast Guard certifications — the real gating factor on automating shipyard work.
insights.speaker: Doug, COO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Certification, not robotics capability, is the binding constraint — a useful milestone test for welding-automation companies.

insights.claim: Reindustrialization requires the government to move first on contracting, because it is a chicken-and-egg problem where commercial industry only invests once demand signals appear — Saronic is fortunate enough to be able to invest ahead of need.
insights.speaker: Doug, COO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Government contracting velocity is the leading indicator for the whole reshoring supply chain, not just for prime contractors.

insights.claim: Trainable-skills programs can radically compress industrial onboarding — a peer company reduced complex wire-harness training from about two years to roughly four weeks — and adults are best taught through apprenticeship and risk/reward skill-building rather than classroom learning.
insights.speaker: host Molly O'Shea and Doug, COO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Suggests the industrial labor bottleneck is compressible on a months-not-years timeline, which materially changes ramp assumptions for manufacturing scale-ups.

insights.claim: This wave of defense acquisition reform is different from prior cycles because there is real money, real teeth and individual-level visibility into where the system breaks — versus the historical pattern of NDAA language producing a report nobody reads while everyone keeps getting promoted.
insights.speaker: Rob, Chief Commercial Officer of Saronic
insights.so_what: If accurate, procurement cycle times compress and non-traditional defense suppliers gain share — the core bull case for the whole defense-tech cohort.
insights.quote: an NDAA piece of language that ultimately yields a report that no one reads and nothing's done about it and people keep moving up the ladder

insights.claim: The binding constraint in defense procurement is that a single contracting officer can veto a program that the program manager, leadership and combatant commander have all aligned on — so accountability structures, not incentives or punishment, are the only lever that actually works on government employees.
insights.speaker: Rob, Chief Commercial Officer of Saronic
insights.so_what: Identifies the precise process choke point to monitor in acquisition-reform legislation — reforms that don't touch contracting-officer authority won't move timelines.
insights.quote: you can't have one human who's not tied to the mission making arbitrary decisions based on a guidebook that doesn't have any wiggle for them

insights.claim: A concrete near-term AI use case in defense is augmenting the acquisition workforce, because contracting officers repeatedly and adamantly insist they cannot do things that new regulations actually permit — they simply are not aware of the maneuver space they have.
insights.speaker: Rob, Chief Commercial Officer of Saronic
insights.so_what: A specific, unglamorous software market inside defense — regulatory-awareness tooling for the acquisition workforce — that would directly shorten procurement cycles.
insights.quote: I think one thing that could help is using AI to augment the acquisition workforce because we've come across multiple times where there's a lack of awareness about a new regulation, a new policy that tells them they can do something that they are adamant that they can't.

insights.claim: Contracting officers default to playing it safe and adhering to old rules because that is what has built their careers, so reform requires giving them a tool that affirmatively tells them a faster path is permitted.
insights.speaker: Rob, Chief Commercial Officer of Saronic
insights.so_what: Explains why top-down policy change alone historically fails to speed procurement — the behavioural layer is where reform succeeds or dies.

insights.claim: Removing humans unlocks an order-of-magnitude performance envelope in boats: commercial vessels are designed around humans tolerating roughly 0.4 to 0.6 Gs, whereas Saronic has seen accelerations north of 20 Gs on its craft.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: The clearest quantification of why unmanned maritime is a step-change rather than an incremental improvement — the physics advantage legacy hulls cannot match.
insights.quote: I think a lot of commercial boats, like you kind of target the human beings to like take like 0.4 to 0.6 Gs maybe. Um you know, our boats like we've seen accelerations north of 20 Gs before.

insights.claim: AI coding tools have inverted the robotics development sequence — because code and debug cycles are now fast, the prudent move is to front-load hardware bench assembly, observability and simulation, so Saronic built Marauder's genset, propulsion stack and bow thruster in a room roughly eight months before the 180-foot ship existed.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: A genuinely non-obvious second-order effect of AI coding: it changes hardware capital-deployment sequencing and compresses time-to-first-mission for robotics companies.
insights.quote: we built all of the internal kind of genset, propulsion stack, bow thruster, all of those components of the ship just in a room before like probably eight months before the ship was built

insights.claim: The operating principle for hardware/software companies is to deliberately slow software down to be more methodical about infrastructure choices while speeding hardware up by buying parts early and building hardware-in-the-loop systems — converging the two development cadences.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: A transferable diligence question for any robotics company: have they converged their hardware and software cadences, or are they still serialized?
insights.quote: hardware engineers tend to measure twice twice and cut once. Software engineers just cut until it looks looks right

insights.claim: Saronic designs to modular open systems with well-known hardware and software APIs specifically so third-party payloads can be integrated quickly — proprietary bespoke protocols or custom plugs make payload integration prohibitively slow.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Open architecture is both a government procurement requirement and a moat-building ecosystem play — a differentiator versus closed prime platforms.

insights.claim: Electronics are designed so cameras and sensors sit on power distribution modules that can be individually power-cycled remotely in software — needed because operators in contested RF environments often must keep radar off to avoid revealing position.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Mission-driven electronics design decisions that legacy manned hulls can't retrofit — a concrete source of technical differentiation.

insights.claim: Every Saronic platform ships with a PACE plan — a redundant set of beyond-line-of-sight and line-of-sight communications including Starlink and its defense variant Starshield — because heavy sea states and water on antennas degrade quality of service the same way active jamming would.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: The ocean itself functions as a permanent jammer, which means maritime autonomy demands comms redundancy that aerial drones can skip — a cost and design burden unique to the domain.
insights.quote: the nice part about the ocean or maybe the bad part about the ocean is that ocean kind of does that for you regardless

insights.claim: Lost-comms behaviour on Saronic vessels is not fixed by the manufacturer but mission-planned by the operator through open APIs — continue the mission, loiter, return to last comms position, or return to base — with responsibility resting on the operator.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Pushing autonomy policy decisions to the operator is how the company sidesteps the regulatory and liability debates that slow autonomous systems approval.

insights.claim: Nvidia dominates robotics compute and Saronic uses it not primarily on price but because the software layer is easiest to move quickly with, and Nvidia's large training-side market share makes the inference-side transition seamless.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Direct practitioner confirmation that Nvidia's robotics moat is CUDA-software lock-in rather than silicon price — relevant to any bear case built on cheaper accelerators.
insights.quote: I think it's a combination of price point, but but predominantly this the software layer is is um just the easiest to to move quickly with

insights.claim: Saronic runs Palantir Foundry as the backbone for its manufacturing execution system and MRP, with an unexpectedly easy adoption curve where supply chain analysts and even PR staff build their own dashboards.
insights.speaker: Doug, COO of Saronic
insights.so_what: A real-world datapoint on Foundry penetration into industrial/manufacturing workflows beyond government analytics — supports the Palantir commercial expansion thesis.

themes.theme: Maritime autonomy's data and regulatory gap

insights.claim: Maritime autonomy lacks the open-source data foundation that UAVs and self-driving cars have — hundreds of billions of dollars have gone into self-driving with open datasets and research, while maritime data is sparse for two reasons: manning requirements on autonomous boats blocked the commercial economic push, and acoustic and subsea perception work gets classified very quickly.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: The data scarcity is itself the moat — whoever accumulates proprietary maritime perception data early has a defensible position that drone makers never got.
insights.quote: You still have manning requirements on autonomous boats so that that you you haven't had the economic push.

insights.claim: Legacy marine engineering software is unusable for small autonomous vessels — one of the largest European marine design firms' simulation software produced numerical instability every single time Saronic tried to design a boat under 50 feet in it.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Incumbent maritime tooling literally cannot model the new product category, forcing from-scratch builds — a barrier to entry and a whitespace for maritime simulation software.
insights.quote: every single time we tried to design a boat under 50 ft in their simulation software, there was numerical instability

insights.claim: Operating at the ocean surface is harder than operating subsea because the surface is a dual-fluid environment — ten feet below the surface is a single, plannable fluid, while the surface produces rare tail-risk events like stuffing the boat on a bad wave at the wrong speed.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Explains why surface autonomy is technically distinct from (and in some ways harder than) subsea — relevant to comparing USV and UUV companies.

insights.claim: Long-duration ocean missions create failure modes absent from land and air robotics: saltwater on antennas degrades quality of service, birds nest on vessels over 30-day missions, and biofouling accumulates.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Sustainment and maintenance cost assumptions for maritime autonomy should not be benchmarked off drone fleets.

insights.claim: Regulatory approval is the gating milestone the company hopes to push through within a year — the goal is autonomous surface vehicles becoming as visible in daily life as Teslas and Waymos on the streets.
insights.speaker: Doug, COO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Regulatory approval, not technology, is the catalyst that would open the commercial maritime market — the specific event to watch.

insights.claim: The moat of the future will be building real, tangible, manufactured things rather than software, precisely because AI and bot coding are commoditizing software.
insights.speaker: Doug, COO of Saronic
insights.so_what: The core allocation argument for hard-tech and manufacturing over pure software as AI compresses software margins — an explicit sector-rotation thesis.
insights.quote: being successful in real space, doing hard tech, building real things, and manufacturing with real tangible items is going to be the moat of the future, especially as software becomes a bit more commoditized

insights.claim: Volume changes the fundamentals of how autonomous systems are used — with five or ten units operators baby each one, but with hundreds of Corsairs or twenty Marauders the operational cadence and the set of possible missions changes entirely, and a fully unmanned fleet has never been done before.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: The step-function value inflection is at fleet scale, not first delivery — the milestone that should re-rate an attritable-mass defense company.
insights.quote: there's a big difference in the operational cadence when you have hundreds of something uh versus when you have like five or 10

insights.claim: The largest untapped opportunity is commercial: the market has not had its aha moment that dramatically reducing the cost of doing things in the ocean opens entirely new categories of activity currently priced out.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: Frames the long-term equity story as a cost-curve-driven market creation play rather than a defense budget share play.
insights.quote: if you reduce the overall cost of doing things in the ocean, um there's so many new cool things that you can get into

insights.claim: The CTO's stated excitement is the wave of open-source AI, on the view that it will democratize tooling and resources and that competitive open ecosystems historically make technology better for everyone, drawing the analogy to how much of the internet rests on a handful of open-source repositories.
insights.speaker: Viv, CTO of Saronic
insights.so_what: A robotics practitioner betting on open-weight models rather than closed frontier labs — signal on where embodied-AI demand may concentrate.

insights.claim: Saronic's systems have already had documented real-world operational impact, with the team seeking to personally thank two Apache pilots affected by the technology in recent weeks.
insights.speaker: Rob, Chief Commercial Officer of Saronic
insights.so_what: Combat-relevant operational proof is the credibility event that converts defense-tech valuations into programs of record.
insights.quote: what I'm looking forward to most is shaking hands with those two Apache pilots
